marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q001.takeaway: Neurites are neuronal processes: one axon and multiple dendrites.
marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q001.displayText:
Neurites (neuronal processes) are the dendrites and the axon. They are projections arising from the cell body (soma) of a neuron.

• An axon is a single, long projection that carries impulses away from the cell body. It ends by dividing into branches called axon terminals, which synapse with dendrites of another neuron, or it may end on an effector such as a muscle or gland. The axon is free of Nissl granules.
• Dendrites are multiple, short projections that carry nerve impulses toward the neuron. Nissl granules are present in dendrites.

The neuronal cytoskeleton consists of neurofilaments and microtubules, which are abundant in the cell body, dendrites and axon. Neurofilaments are protein heteropolymers that give tensile strength to the axon; bundles of neurofilaments form a neurofibril. Microtubules assist axonal transport.

rationales.a: Neurofibrils are cytoskeletal bundles within neuronal processes, not one of the two neurite types.
rationales.c: Neurofibrils are cytoskeletal structures; the neurites are the axon and dendrites.
rationales.d: This adds neurofibrils, which are cytoskeletal bundles, to the two neurite classes: axons and dendrites.

marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q002.takeaway: The axon hillock is the Nissl-free region of the neuron cell body where the axon begins.
marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q002.displayText:
The Nissl-free zone from which the axon arises is the axon hillock.

Nissl bodies (Nissl granules) are aggregates of polyribosomes and rough endoplasmic reticulum. They are present in the cell body and large dendrites of a neuron. Under light microscopy they appear as basophilic granules because they contain abundant acidic RNA, which has affinity for basic dyes. The source image shows blue Nissl bodies in motor-neuron cytoplasm.

• The initial segment is the proximal part of the axon just beyond the axon hillock. The hillock is part of the cell body; the initial segment is part of the axon.
• The mesaxon is where the Schwann-cell plasma membrane fuses with itself as it wraps around the axon to form the myelin sheath. The Schwann-cell cytoplasm and nucleus are pushed to the periphery; the thin Schwann-cell cytoplasm surrounding the sheath is the neurilemma.
• Each Schwann cell myelinates a short axon segment. The unmyelinated gaps between segments are nodes of Ranvier.

rationales.a: The initial segment is the proximal axon beyond the hillock; the hillock itself is the Nissl-free region on the cell body.
rationales.b: Mesaxon is the fused Schwann-cell membrane that wraps around an axon during myelination.
rationales.d: Nodes of Ranvier are gaps between myelinated segments, not the Nissl-free origin of the axon.

marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q003.takeaway: Osmium tetroxide makes myelin black by reacting with unsaturated fatty acids.
marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q003.displayText:
The stain used in the nerve section is osmium tetroxide. It is reduced to a black substance by unsaturated fatty acids in the myelin sheath, so myelin appears black.

Pure neuritic leprosy is a variant involving peripheral nerve trunks in the absence of skin lesions. Nerve biopsy is the gold-standard method for diagnosis of this form.

rationales.a: Sudan Black can stain lipids, but the source identifies osmium tetroxide for this nerve section and notes that it blackens myelin.
rationales.b: Giemsa is not the stain identified here; osmium tetroxide reacts with myelin’s unsaturated fatty acids.
rationales.d: Silver stain is not the source-identified myelin stain in this section; osmium tetroxide renders myelin black.

marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q004.takeaway: On H&E, myelinated fibers show empty spaces where myelin was not stained; unmyelinated fibers do not.
marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q004.displayText:
In the cross-sectional H&E images, image A shows an unmyelinated nerve fiber, identified by the absence of empty spaces around the fibers. Image B shows a myelinated nerve fiber, identified by empty spaces around the fibers (arrows).

H&E does not color myelin, which appears as a white region or empty space around the nerve fiber. Special myelin stains such as Luxol fast blue and Sudan blue stain myelin with less intensity. Osmium tetroxide stains myelin black.

rationales.a: This reverses the image findings: A is unmyelinated and B is myelinated.
rationales.c: Image A lacks the periaxonal empty space and is unmyelinated; only B is myelinated.
rationales.d: Image B has empty spaces around its fibers, identifying myelin; therefore both are not unmyelinated.

marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q005.takeaway: The cerebellar cortex runs molecular → Purkinje → granular, with white matter deep to it.
marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q005.displayText:
The labeled cerebellar structures are:
• A — molecular layer
• B — Purkinje layer
• C — granular layer
• D — white matter

The cerebellum is covered by pia mater, seen as thin connective tissue with blood vessels beneath it. It consists of outer gray matter (the cerebellar cortex) and inner white matter.

rationales.a: This mapping places B in the granular layer, but B marks the Purkinje layer; C marks the granular layer.
rationales.c: A marks the molecular layer and B the Purkinje layer; the option swaps A and the Purkinje assignment.
rationales.d: A is the molecular layer and B the Purkinje layer, so their labels are not as given here.

marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q006.takeaway: The six cerebral cortical layers from superficial to deep are molecular, external granular, external pyramidal, internal granular, ganglionic and multiform.
marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q006.displayText:
From superficial to deep, the cerebral cortex layers are:
1. Molecular layer (plexiform layer)
2. External granular layer
3. External pyramidal layer
4. Internal granular layer, containing the outer band of Baillarger
5. Ganglionic layer (internal pyramidal layer), containing the inner band of Baillarger
6. Multiform layer (layer of polymorphic cells)

rationales.a: This puts the external pyramidal layer before the external granular layer and misorders the deep layers.
rationales.b: This places the multiform layer second, but it is the deepest layer; the external granular and pyramidal layers are also reversed.
rationales.d: This places the multiform layer second and misorders the external and internal layers; the correct superficial-to-deep sequence is 1-4-2-3-6-5.

marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q007.takeaway: The outer band of Baillarger is in layer IV (internal granular); in visual cortex it forms the stria of Gennari.
marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q007.displayText:
The outer band of Baillarger is in the internal granular layer (layer IV) of the cerebral cortex.

Cerebral cortical nerve fibers run radially and tangentially. Tangential fibers are concentrated in the internal granular layer (outer band of Baillarger) and ganglionic layer (layer V; inner band of Baillarger). These bands are well developed in sensory areas because of the terminal parts of thalamocortical fibers. In the visual cortex, the outer band can be seen with the naked eye and is called the stria of Gennari; this gives the visual cortex the name striate cortex. The source image shows the bands of Baillarger/stria of Gennari and subcortical white matter at the bottom.

rationales.a: The external pyramidal layer is layer III, not the internal granular layer containing the outer band.
rationales.c: The internal pyramidal (ganglionic) layer contains the inner band of Baillarger, not the outer band.
rationales.d: The external granular layer is layer II; the outer band of Baillarger is in the internal granular layer (IV).

marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q008.takeaway: Pituitary lactotrophs are acidophils that produce prolactin and stain pink with eosin.
marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q008.displayText:
Prolactin-producing pituitary cells are acidophils and stain with eosin.

The pituitary gland has pars anterior, pars intermedia and pars posterior (pars nervosa). Pars anterior (pars distalis) contains chromophil and chromophobe cells. Chromophils have brightly staining cytoplasmic granules:
• Acidophils (alpha cells) stain with acidic dyes such as eosin or orange G and appear pink on H&E. Somatotrophs produce growth hormone; lactotrophs produce prolactin.
• Basophils (beta cells) stain with basic dyes such as hematoxylin and appear blue on H&E. They are PAS-positive; corticotrophs produce ACTH, thyrotrophs produce TSH, and gonadotrophs produce FSH and LH.
• Chromophobes lack stainable granules and appear colorless on H&E.

Pars intermedia contains colloid-filled vesicles, remnants of Rathke’s pouch. Pars posterior contains hypothalamic neuronal fibers and supporting pituicytes.

rationales.a: Thyrotrophs produce TSH and are basophils, which stain with basic dyes rather than eosin.
rationales.b: Corticotrophs produce ACTH and are basophils, not eosin-staining acidophils.
rationales.d: Gonadotrophs produce FSH/LH and are basophils; prolactin-producing lactotrophs are acidophils.

marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q009.takeaway: Age-related pineal calcification (corpora arenacea) can appear as a radio-opacity on skull X-ray.
marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q009.displayText:
The radio-opacity at the pineal gland is most likely corpora arenacea (brain sand). These structures within the pineal gland calcify increasingly with age, are visible on X-ray, and can serve as landmarks. Their deposits may contain calcium phosphate, magnesium phosphate, calcium carbonate and ammonium phosphate.

Pinealocytes are the gland’s cells; they produce melatonin, which works with the hypothalamus in sleep–wake regulation. Corpora amylacea are small eosinophilic inclusions reported in histologic sections of the brain, prostate, lung and uterus. The source image shows darkly stained corpora arenacea in the pineal gland.

rationales.a: Pinealocytes are melatonin-producing cells, not the age-calcifying bodies that create the radiopacity.
rationales.c: Nervi conarii are nerve structures associated with the pineal region, not the calcifying pineal bodies called corpora arenacea.
rationales.d: Corpora amylacea are eosinophilic inclusions in several tissues; the source identifies pineal calcifications as corpora arenacea.

marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q010.takeaway: Thyroid C-cells are parafollicular cells that secrete calcitonin.
marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q010.displayText:
The structure marked X is a C-cell (parafollicular cell) of the thyroid. C-cells lie between follicular cells and the basement membrane or between follicles and secrete calcitonin.

The fibrous thyroid capsule sends septa that divide the gland into lobules containing follicles lined by follicular cells. Follicular cell shape varies with gland activity: cells are squamous when inactive and cuboidal to columnar when active. Follicular colloid appears pink with H&E.

Hürthle cells are oncocytes derived from follicular cells. They have eosinophilic granular cytoplasm and a vesicular nucleus with a large nucleolus and occur in Hashimoto thyroiditis, Hürthle-cell adenoma and carcinoma.

marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q011.takeaway: Oxyphil cells are larger and eosinophilic; chief cells are numerous and produce parathormone.
marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q011.displayText:
The marked structures are A, oxyphil cells, and B, chief cells. The clinical history and MRI findings suggest primary hyperparathyroidism due to a parathyroid adenoma.

The parathyroid gland has two cell types:
• Chief (principal) cells are small and round, with vesicular nuclei and little cytoplasm. They are numerous and produce parathormone.
• Oxyphil cells are fewer and scattered among chief cells. They are larger, have smaller nuclei and eosinophilic (pink) cytoplasm; their function is not known.

Primary hyperparathyroidism is usually due to a solitary parathyroid adenoma. Associated clinical signs can be recalled as “bones, stones, groans, moans, with fatigue overtones.”

rationales.b: B marks chief cells, not follicular cells; the gland shown is parathyroid.
rationales.d: This reverses the structures: A is oxyphil and B is chief, not the other way around.

marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q012.takeaway: Zona fasciculata cells form straight columns separated by sinusoids.
marrow__ANAT_CH13_Q012.displayText:
The cells are arranged in straight columns in the zona fasciculata. From outermost to deepest, the adrenal cortex has three layers:
• Zona glomerulosa — small polyhedral cells arranged in inverted U-shaped formations or acinus-like groups; produces mineralocorticoids.
• Zona fasciculata — straight columns of cells with sinusoids between them; produces glucocorticoids.
• Zona reticularis — branching and anastomosing cell columns form a reticulum; produces sex hormones (progesterone, estrogens and androgens).

rationales.b: Zona glomerulosa cells form inverted U-shaped or acinus-like groups and produce mineralocorticoids.
rationales.c: Zona reticularis cells branch and anastomose into a network; they do not form straight columns.
rationales.d: The adrenal medulla is not a layer of the cortex, and the described straight columns identify zona fasciculata.
